claim: In response to central nervous system (CNS) injury, tissue-resident immune cells such as microglia and circulating systemic neutrophils are often first responders.
source: In response to central nervous system (CNS) injury, tissue-resident immune cells such as microglia and circulating systemic neutrophils are often first responders.
evidence: This is a general statement about CNS injury response that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The degree to which microglia and neutrophils interact in response to CNS damage is poorly understood.
source: The degree to which these cells interact in response to CNS damage is poorly understood, and even less so, in the neural retina, which poses a challenge for high-resolution imaging in vivo.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Retinal lesions induced with 488 nm light focused onto photoreceptor outer segments focally ablated PRs with minimal collateral damage to cells above and below the plane of focus.
source: Retinal lesions were induced with 488 nm light focused onto photoreceptor (PR) outer segments. These lesions focally ablated PRs, with minimal collateral damage to cells above and below the plane of focus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript, including OCT and histological data showing confined damage.

claim: Microglia migrated into the injury locus within 1 day after injury.
source: While microglia showed dynamic and progressive immune response with cells migrating into the injury locus within 1 day after injury, neutrophils were not recruited despite close proximity to vessels carrying neutrophils only microns away.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo AOSLO imaging data and ex vivo confocal microscopy showing microglial migration.

claim: Neutrophils were not recruited despite close proximity to vessels carrying neutrophils only microns away from the injury site.
source: While microglia showed dynamic and progressive immune response with cells migrating into the injury locus within 1 day after injury, neutrophils were not recruited despite close proximity to vessels carrying neutrophils only microns away.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo AOSLO imaging and ex vivo confocal microscopy showing absence of neutrophil extravasation.

claim: Microglial activation does not recruit neutrophils in response to acute, focal loss of PRs.
source: This work illustrates that microglial activation does not recruit neutrophils in response to acute, focal loss of PRs, a condition encountered in many retinal diseases.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing microglial activation without neutrophil recruitment.

claim: Mature retinal neurons do not typically regenerate, resulting in long-term functional losses for the host.
source: This is especially critical in the eye since mature retinal neurons do not typically regenerate, resulting in long-term functional losses for the host (Stone et al., 1999; García-Ayuso et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The retina is considered immune-privileged.
source: The retina is considered immune-privileged and is equipped with a resident population of innate immune cells, including microglia (Boycott and Hopkins, 1981; Silverman and Wong, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In healthy retina, microglia are distributed primarily in the inner retina, residing within nerve fiber layer (NFL), inner plexiform layer (IPL), and outer plexiform layer (OPL).
source: In healthy retina, microglia are distributed primarily in the inner retina, residing within nerve fiber layer (NFL), inner plexiform layer (IPL), and outer plexiform layer (OPL) (Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), generally avoiding the nuclear layers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia generally avoid the nuclear layers in healthy retina.
source: In healthy retina, microglia are distributed primarily in the inner retina, residing within nerve fiber layer (NFL), inner plexiform layer (IPL), and outer plexiform layer (OPL) (Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), generally avoiding the nuclear layers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia exhibit long, thin processes that continually probe the neuro-glial microenvironment.
source: Microglia tile the retina and, like their counterparts in the brain, exhibit long, thin processes that continually probe the neuro-glial microenvironment (Silverman and Wong, 2018; Joseph et al., 2021; Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neutrophils comprise a large fraction (20–30%) of leukocytes in murine blood.
source: Neutrophils comprise a large fraction (20–30%) of leukocytes in murine blood (Provencher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 1 day post-488 nm light exposure, both near-infrared (NIR) and blue reflectance modalities showed hyperreflective lesions, most apparent at a deeper retinal focus position.
source: 1 day post-488 nm light exposure, both near-infrared (NIR) and blue reflectance modalities showed hyperreflective lesions, most apparent at a deeper retinal focus position.
evidence: This is supported by SLO imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Despite deep retinal damage, fluorescein angiography did not reveal dye leakage, indicating the blood–retinal barrier remained intact.
source: Despite deep retinal damage, fluorescein angiography did not reveal dye leakage (Figure 1B, bottom), indicating the blood–retinal barrier remained intact.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescein angiography data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Within 30 minutes post-laser exposure, OCT revealed a zone of hyperreflection within the ONL.
source: Within 30 minutes post-laser exposure, OCT revealed a zone of hyperreflection within the ONL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by OCT imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1 day post-lesion, the focal hyperreflection remained localized to the ONL (~50 µm wide).
source: 1 day post-lesion, the focal hyperreflection remained localized to the ONL (~50 µm wide, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by OCT imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The hyperreflective phenotype persisted through 7 days and was cleared by 2 months.
source: The hyperreflective phenotype persisted through 7 days and was cleared by 2 months (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal OCT imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There did not appear to be any cellular excavation, 'cratering,' or evidence of edema for any time point assessed.
source: There did not appear to be any cellular excavation, 'cratering,' or evidence of edema for any time point assessed.
evidence: This is based on OCT imaging observations across multiple time points.

claim: Bruch's membrane appeared intact for all time points.
source: Bruch's membrane appeared intact for all time points, evidenced by lack of fluorescein leakage at the site of lesion.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescein angiography data.

claim: The dense packing of individual PR somata was disrupted 1 day post-exposure (~50 µm ovoid), suggesting degradation or ablation of the cell membrane.
source: We found that the dense packing of individual somata was disrupted 1 day post-exposure (~50 µm ovoid, Figure 2C), suggesting degradation or ablation of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is supported by phase-contrast AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 1 day after laser exposure, mild thickening of the ONL was observed compared to unexposed locations.
source: 1 day after laser exposure, we observed mild thickening of the ONL compared to unexposed locations only microns away.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 3 and 7 days, local ONL thinning was observed.
source: At 3 and 7 days, local ONL thinning was observed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: By 2 months, the lesion's overall appearance and ONL thickness returned to baseline.
source: By 2 months, the lesion's overall appearance and ONL thickness returned to baseline (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: At 3 and 7 days post-exposure, there was a corresponding reduction in the density of ONL nuclei of 18% and 27%, respectively.
source: In comparison to control locations (501,317 nuclei/mm2±46,198 nuclei/mm2, mean ± SD, similar to previous work; Jeon et al., 1998), at 3 and 7 days post-exposure, we found a corresponding reduction in the density of ONL nuclei of 18% (408,965 nuclei/mm2±25,621 nuclei/mm2) and 27% (367,542 nuclei/mm2±9038 nuclei/mm2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DAPI-stained tissue.

claim: 2 months after damage, PR nuclear densities were indistinguishable from that of control.
source: 2 months after damage, PR nuclear densities were indistinguishable from that of control (Figure 3F, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Total cell nuclei within the INL remained unchanged for all time points.
source: Despite losses of PR nuclei, total cell nuclei within the INL remained unchanged for all time points (Figure 3F, black bars).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The laser exposure focally ablated PRs whilst leaving inner retinal cells intact.
source: These data indicate that the laser exposure focally ablated PRs whilst leaving inner retinal cells intact.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the histological data showing ONL loss but preserved INL.

claim: Motion contrast images revealed that the vasculature remained perfused from hours to months after laser damage.
source: Motion contrast (Chui et al., 2012; Guevara-Torres et al., 2016) images revealed that the vasculature remained perfused from hours to months after laser damage, suggesting that acute or long-term changes are not imparted by the laser injury (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by motion contrast imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: None of the primary vascular stratifications within the NFL, IPL, and OPL of the mouse retina showed stopped flow as a result of the laser lesion.
source: None of the primary vascular stratifications within the NFL, IPL, and OPL of the mouse retina (Schallek et al., 2013) showed stopped flow as a result of the laser lesion, reinforcing the findings above regarding the axial confinement of the damage to the outer retina.
evidence: This is supported by motion contrast imaging data.

claim: Blood cell flux for capillaries within lesion locations was within the range of normal flux for the C57BL/6 J mouse.
source: Blood cell flux for capillaries within lesion locations was within the range of normal flux for the C57BL/6 J mouse (Dholakia et al., 2022; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of capillary flux shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1 day after injury, SLO revealed bright, focal congregations of microglia at injury locations in contrast to undamaged locations, which maintained a distribution of lateral tiling.
source: 1 day after injury, SLO revealed bright, focal congregations of microglia at injury locations in contrast to undamaged locations, which maintained a distribution of lateral tiling (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by SLO imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Laser-damaged locations showed a congregation of cells 1 day post-injury with less lateral ramification.
source: Whereas AOSLO imaging of microglia in the healthy retina displayed a distributed array of microglia with ramified processes (Figure 5C, left), laser-damaged locations showed a congregation of cells 1 day post-injury with less lateral ramification (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Within hours of the laser exposure, there was no observed photo-bleaching or death of regional microglia.
source: Within hours of the laser exposure, we did not observe a photo-bleaching or death of regional microglia, suggesting that while the laser exposure was sufficient to damage PRs, it left retinal microglia intact.
evidence: This is based on AOSLO imaging observations.

claim: At 1 day post-injury, damage locations displayed aggregations of microglia with surrounding microglia displaying process polarization with extensions projecting toward the injury.
source: At 1 day post-injury, damage locations displayed aggregations of microglia. The surrounding microglia displayed process polarization with extensions projecting toward the injury (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: By days 3 and 7, microglia exhibited fewer lateral projections and somas have migrated into the ONL where they do not normally reside.
source: By days 3 and 7, microglia exhibited fewer lateral projections and somas have migrated into the ONL where they do not normally reside (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: By 2 months post-injury, the hyperreflective phenotype was absent and microglia once again occupied only the inner retina.
source: By 2 months post-injury, the hyperreflective phenotype was absent and microglia once again occupied only the inner retina.
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The hyperreflective phenotype appeared within 30 minutes but microglia were not found to aggregate until 1 day post-damage.
source: The hyperreflective phenotype appeared within 30 minutes but microglia were not found to aggregate until 1 day post-damage.
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microglia are not the initial source of the lesion-induced hyperreflective appearance.
source: During these time points, simultaneously imaged microglia remained ramified and maintained a tiled arrangement, indicating that microglia are not the initial source of the lesion-induced hyperreflective appearance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from simultaneous imaging of hyperreflectivity and microglia shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no evidence of neutrophil involvement at the times examined (1-, 3-, 7-day, and 2-month follow-up).
source: While we observed a robust microglial response to PR damage, there was no evidence of neutrophil involvement at the times we examined (1-, 3-, 7-day, and 2-month follow-up).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo AOSLO imaging and ex vivo confocal microscopy.

claim: Neutrophils show deformation within the small confines of the capillary lumen, often resulting in tube or pill-shaped morphology.
source: We found that neutrophils show deformation within the small confines of the capillary lumen, often resulting in tube or pill-shaped morphology seen both in vivo and ex vivo (Figure 7B, top).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: After laser lesion, there was no evidence of neutrophil aggregation or extravasation for any time point assessed.
source: After laser lesion, we found no evidence of neutrophil aggregation or extravasation for any time point assessed (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by AOSLO imaging data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a notable lack of rolling/crawling neutrophils (or any putative leukocyte) in large arterioles or venules surrounding the injury.
source: There was also a notable lack of rolling/crawling neutrophils (or any putative leukocyte) in large arterioles or venules surrounding the injury (Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by video imaging data referenced as Figure 8—video 1.

claim: Neutrophils closest to the ONL lesion were occasionally detected within the deepest retinal capillaries but stayed within the retinal vasculature.
source: Neutrophils closest to the ONL lesion were occasionally detected within the deepest retinal capillaries. However, these neutrophils stayed within the retinal vasculature, as evidenced by their pill-shaped morphology and passage routes that follow the known vascular paths seen in confocal/phase-contrast images (Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by video imaging data referenced as Figure 8—video 2.

claim: In the EIU model, an abundance of neutrophils was found within the retinal parenchyma 1 day after LPS injection.
source: With fluorescence AOSLO (Figure 7—video 3) and ex vivo confocal microscopy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), we found an abundance of neutrophils within the retinal parenchyma 1 day after LPS injection.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from the EIU positive control model.

claim: Neutrophils that have extravasated into the retinal parenchyma tended to have a more spherical morphology rather than the compressed, pill-shaped morphology of neutrophils within capillaries.
source: Moreover, we found that neutrophils that have extravasated into the retinal parenchyma tended to have a more spherical morphology rather than the compressed, pill-shaped morphology of neutrophils within capillaries (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 1 day after laser exposure, microglial somas aggregated to the lesion location and began to migrate into the ONL.
source: 1 day after laser exposure, microglial somas aggregated to the lesion location. They began to migrate into the ONL and changed from the ramified morphology seen in the healthy retina, to a dagger-like axial morphology (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: At 3 and 7 days after lesion, microglia migrated deeper into the outer retina and remained aggregated with an axially elongated phenotype.
source: At 3 and 7 days after lesion, microglia migrated deeper into the outer retina and remained aggregated with an axially elongated phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: 2 months after lesion, microglial somas were no longer found in the ONL and redistributed similar to that of the healthy retina.
source: 2 months after lesion, microglial somas were no longer found in the ONL. Instead, microglia redistributed similar to that of the healthy retina, once again co-stratifying predominantly with the NFL and plexiform layers of the retina (Figure 9A and B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9A and B, and Video 1.

claim: Amoeboid cells enveloped the somata of PRs, and phagocytosis was detected 1, 3, and 7 days post-laser exposure.
source: Amoeboid cells enveloped the somata of PRs, and phagocytosis was detected 1, 3, and 7 days post-laser exposure (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microglia had a nuclear volume of 110±42 µm³ and PR nuclei were 35±5 µm³.
source: Microglia had a nuclear volume of 110±42 µm (Boycott and Hopkins, 1981) and PR nuclei were 35±5 µm (Boycott and Hopkins, 1981) (p<0.001, Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Neutrophils were found within the vascular network and did not extravasate into the neural retina in ex vivo microscopy.
source: Ex vivo microscopy revealed that neutrophils were found within the vascular network and did not extravasate into the neural retina.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo confocal microscopy observations.

claim: Control locations had 15±8 neutrophils per mm² of retina, whereas lesioned locations had 23±5 neutrophils per mm² of retina.
source: Control locations (n=2 mice, four z-stacks) had 15±8 neutrophils per mm2 of retina, whereas lesioned locations (n=2 mice, four z-stacks) had 23±5 neutrophils per mm2 of retina (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The difference between control and lesioned groups was not statistically significant (p=0.19).
source: The difference between control and lesioned groups was not statistically significant (p=0.19).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of neutrophil counts.

claim: Light damage offers placement precision that is better controlled than other invasive methods, such as incision/poke injuries, retinal detachment, and chemical injury.
source: Light damage offers a number of advantages for creating acute damage in the retina. It offers placement precision that is better controlled than other invasive methods, such as incision/poke injuries (Senut et al., 2004), retinal detachment (Maidana et al., 2021), and chemical injury (Wan et al., 2008; Rösch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to other methods.

claim: The amount of light delivered did not immediately ablate PRs as peak cell loss was not observed until 3–7 days after laser exposure, suggesting a progressive damage phenotype of apoptosis or necroptotic death.
source: The amount of light delivered did not immediately ablate PRs as peak cell loss was not observed until 3–7 days after laser exposure, suggesting a progressive damage phenotype of apoptosis or necroptotic death.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the temporal pattern of cell loss observed in histological data.

claim: The total number of PR nuclei within the lesion location returned to values similar to baseline by 2 months, which was surprising given that PRs do not regenerate.
source: The total number of PR nuclei within the lesion location returned to values similar to baseline by 2 months, which was surprising given that PRs do not regenerate.
evidence: This observation is based on histological data and is noted as surprising by the authors.

claim: Adjacent PRs spill into the region of loss, similar to what others have described previously.
source: Our interpretation is that adjacent PRs spill into the region of loss, similar to what others have described previously (Strazzeri et al., 2014; Busch et al., 1999).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous research showing similar phenomena.

claim: The hyperreflective bands appeared within 30 minutes after the laser injury, preceding any detectable microglial migration toward the damage location.
source: We found that the hyperreflective bands appeared within 30 minutes after the laser injury, preceding any detectable microglial migration toward the damage location (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by temporal imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial hyperreflective phenotype is not caused by microglial cell activity or aggregation.
source: We thus conclude that the initial hyperreflective phenotype is not caused by microglial cell activity or aggregation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the temporal sequence showing hyperreflectivity before microglial aggregation.

claim: The lesion did not compromise the blood–retinal barrier or impart perfusion changes within the retinal vasculature.
source: Altogether, these three lines of evidence indicate that the lesion did not compromise the blood–retinal barrier or impart perfusion changes within the retinal vasculature.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from fluorescein angiography, motion-contrast imaging, and capillary flux measurements.

claim: Microglia undergo a rapid and progressive response to this injury, including evidence of PR phagocytosis.
source: We find that microglia undergo a rapid and progressive response to this injury. We show evidence of PR phagocytosis (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), interaction with neighboring microglia (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and they are also axially positioned to facilitate retinal remodeling (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Throughout the temporal evolution of the microglial response, there is no evidence of neutrophil recruitment despite the damage being within 10s of microns from retinal vessels that carry them.
source: Furthermore, throughout the temporal evolution of the microglial response, we find no evidence of neutrophil recruitment despite the damage being within 10s of microns from retinal vessels that carry them.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo and ex vivo imaging data showing absence of neutrophil extravasation.

claim: Although microglia show a strong and lasting activation, at no time point from seconds to months are the damage-associated molecular patterns or chemotactic gradients strong enough to recruit neutrophils in response to this damage.
source: Based on our data, we suggest that although microglia show a strong and lasting activation, at no time point from seconds to months are the damage-associated molecular patterns or chemotactic gradients strong enough to recruit neutrophils in response to this damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the absence of neutrophil recruitment despite microglial activation.

claim: Resident microglia facilitate the necessary phagocytic and retinal remodeling response despite release of cytokines from damaged retinal cells that would normally recruit systemic immune cells in peripheral tissues.
source: It is possible that resident microglia facilitate the necessary phagocytic and retinal remodeling response despite release of cytokines from damaged retinal cells that would normally recruit systemic immune cells in peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Microglia may be involved in a system that protects the CNS from propagating a larger systemic response.
source: Microglia may be involved in a system that protects the CNS from propagating a larger systemic response, potentially exacerbating disease pathologies that would compromise overall CNS function.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and cited work.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages may exhibit the capacity to cloak tissue micro-damage.
source: In another damage model (Uderhardt et al., 2019), they report that tissue-resident macrophages may exhibit the capacity to cloak tissue micro-damage.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Despite a robust microglial activation that lasts for weeks, at no time point do they recruit neutrophils.
source: Regardless of the mechanism, we find that despite a robust microglial activation that lasts for weeks, at no time point do they recruit neutrophils.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: AOSLO cellular-level imaging may reveal the interaction of multiple immune cell types in the living retina.
source: Beyond the context of this specific finding, we share this work with the excitement that AOSLO cellular-level imaging may reveal the interaction of multiple immune cell types in the living retina.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the potential of the imaging technology.

claim: All experiments were approved by the University Committee on Animal Resources (protocol #: UCAR-2010-052E).
source: All experiments herein were approved by the University Committee on Animal Resources (protocol #: UCAR-2010-052E) and according to the Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research as well as institutional approvals by the University of Rochester.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the research.

claim: 18 mice (10 males, 8 females) in total were used for in vivo imaging.
source: 18 mice (10 males, 8 females) in total were used for in vivo imaging.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental sample size.

claim: 10 additional mice (5 males, 5 females) were used for ex vivo histology.
source: 10 additional mice (5 males, 5 females) were used for ex vivo histology.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental sample size.

claim: Ages for all mice used for this work were postnatal weeks 6–24.
source: Ages for all mice used for this work were postnatal weeks 6–24.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: 785 µW of 488 nm light was projected through the AOSLO and focused onto the PR outer segments for 3 minutes in a single line on the retina subtending 24 × 1 µm.
source: 785 µW of 488 nm light was projected through the AOSLO and focused onto the PR outer segments (Figure 1A) for 3 minutes in a single line on the retina subtending 24 × 1 µm to concentrate the power to a small region.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method for creating laser lesions.

claim: This protocol produced a hyper-reflective phenotype in >40 locations across 28 mice.
source: This protocol produced a hyper-reflective phenotype in the >40 locations across 28 mice.
evidence: This is a statement about the reproducibility of the lesion protocol.
